title: Private VPC control plane reachability — incident review & runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working incident review and runbook draft for the Nov 11, 2025 control-plane reachability incidents affecting a handful of Private/VPC deployments. Impact: customers with on-prem or VPC deployments intermittently lost ability to reach the Redwood control plane (API and health checks) for 30–90s windows, causing agent reconnections and a small number of customer failovers. Not a data compromise, but degraded orchestration and rollout failures.

High-level cause hypothesis (short):
- Combination of over-restrictive customer firewall rule changes + our control-plane egress IP rotation combined with an edge NAT translation change in a customer VPC. Result: asymmetric routing + TCP resets between control plane and customer agents.

Why this is important:
- Private deployments rely on stable reachability for rolling updates, metrics, and orchestration. Short control-plane gaps cascade into agent restarts and customer-visible errors. Need a reproducible runbook for detection and mitigation, and clearer customer-facing network guidance.

Timeline (reconstructed from logs + on-call notes):
- 2025-11-11 01:12 UTC — First alert: increased agent reconnection rate from 3 customers (alert SRE-ctrlplane-conn-rate).
- 01:13 UTC — Pager on-call (Morgan) investigates; control plane frontends showing increased FIN/RST rates to client IP ranges.
- 01:15 UTC — Customers report transient errors in rollout agent logs (connectivity errors, TLS handshake failures).
- 01:18 UTC — On-call runs quick traceroutes and curl checks from control plane to customer egress IPs (see commands below).
- 01:22 UTC — Noticed spike in control plane NAT gateway errors in cloud region us-west-2; edge team rolling kernel micro-update at 01:20 UTC suspected but not yet confirmed.
- 01:30 UTC — Customer network team confirms firewall rule change around 01:16 UTC (temporary tighten of allowed ephemeral ports for outgoing connections).
- 01:36 UTC — Engineering mitigations: temporarily pinned control-plane egress IPs via policy and opened support firewall window with customer. Reachability recovered for most customers by 01:44 UTC.
- 02:05 UTC — Post-incident triage started.

Observed symptoms and evidence:
- Agent logs (customer): repeated errors: "connection reset by peer", "TLS handshake timed out".
- Control plane logs: elevated TCP RST counts to customer egress IP blocks, SYN re-transmissions 4x baseline.
- Cloud VPC NAT logs: transient failures 01:19–01:25 UTC; host-level NAT table rotation noted at 01:20 UTC (kernel upgrade + iptables reload by infra).
- Customer firewall change: blocked ephemeral outbound ports > 32768 for a short window (customer change ticket #NET-2025-11-11).

Root cause analysis (working):
- Contributing factor 1: Customer firewall tightened outbound ephemeral port range, blocking the high source ports used by our control-plane connections back to the agent during symmetric NAT traversal.
- Contributing factor 2: Simultaneous iptables / NAT translation reload on our egress hosts caused brief change in mapping behaviour; combined with the firewall change, this caused a window where TCP sessions were reset.
- Contributing factor 3: Our monitoring alert thresholds are based on long-window averages; they detected the problem but did not clearly surface asymmetric routing or NAT-related failures as a distinct category.

Immediate mitigation performed:
- Communication: Slack bridge to customer network ops to coordinate a temporary exception.
- Infrastructure: Pinned a stable egress IP range for the affected control-plane pool while infra rolled back the iptables reload sweep.
- Customers: Advised short-lived firewall exception for control-plane egress IPs and expanded ephemeral port range for outbound traffic for 10 minutes.

Suggested runbook draft (steps to include in a formal runbook):
- Pager receives SRE-ctrlplane-conn-rate or agent-reconnect spike.
- Step 0: Confirm scope. Query: 
  - curl https://internal-api.redwood/health/controlplane (internal) 
  - kubectl -n controlplane logs frontend-<pod> | grep RST | tail -n 100
  - grep -E "RST|FIN" /var/log/controlplane/tcp_stats.log | tail -n 200
- Step 1: Compare agent-side vs control-plane side TCP metrics. Use netstat/tcpdump snippets if needed: 
  - tcpdump -nni eth0 host <customer_egress_ip> and port 443 -w /tmp/trace.pcap (run 60s)
  - sudo ss -tnp dst <customer_egress_ip> sport = :443
- Step 2: From control plane host, run traceroute and mtr to customer egress IP: 
  - traceroute -T -p 443 <customer_egress_ip>
  - mtr --tcp -P 443 -i 0.5 <customer_egress_ip>
- Step 3: Ask customer to check their firewall outbound ephemeral port policy and NAT behaviour. Provide recommended checks (from runbook appendix).
- Step 4: If firewall change suspected and customer permits, suggest temporary allow for our control-plane egress CIDR and broaden ephemeral port range to 1024–65535 (or at least > 32768).
- Step 5: If infra Nat/gateway reload suspected, work with infra to roll back or reapply in a staged way. Pin egress IPs for affected pool and advertise pinned range to customer for a short maintenance window.
- Step 6: Post-recovery: collect tcpdump, pcap, control-plane logs, and customer firewall logs for a 15-minute window. Attach to Jira ticket.

Troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- Can the control plane reach the customer egress IP? 
  - curl -vI --resolve api.redwood-internal:<port>:<customer_egress_ip> https://api.redwood-internal:<port>/health 
- Do we see asymmetric packet loss vs packet resets? Check tcpdump for RSTs from both sides.
- Is there NAT timeout or mapping churn? Compare source port translations before/after connection attempt.
- Was there any infra maintenance around the timestamp (k8s daemonset updates, iptables reload, kernel updates)? Check infra-change log.

Customer-facing guidance snippet (to be added to support FAQ):
- Requirements for reaching Redwood control plane:
  - Allow outbound TLS to control-plane egress CIDRs on port 443 (TCP).
  - Allow ephemeral outbound source ports range at minimum 32768–65535. If customer NATs with restricted mapping, allow broader range or use static source NAT for agent hosts.
  - If using stateful firewall appliances, ensure return traffic allowed for established sessions and that SYN/ACKs are not blocked by asymmetric routing.
  - Recommend keeping a maintenance window for firewall rule changes and coordinating with Redwood for egress IP changes.

Runbook appendix — example customer checks to request:
- Provide a short command set the customer can run: 
  - sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 host <control_plane_egress_ip> and port 443 
  - iptables -t nat -L -n -v  # show SNAT rules
  - cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack | grep <control_plane_egress_ip>
  - show firewall policy <policy-id> | include ephemeral

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Why did our egress hosts rotate NAT mappings at 01:20? Infra confirmed an iptables reload but we need exact change log entry from release-engineering.
- Do we need a persistent pinned egress pool for all Private customers to avoid this class of issue? Cost/scale analysis required.
- Can we detect asymmetric routing/NAT-induced resets automatically and emit a specialized alert? (SRE-alert idea: ctrlplane-nat-reset-rate > threshold).

Action items (owner, ETA):
- Aisha: collect / share precise infra-syslog for iptables reload (ETA 2025-11-15).
- Diego: draft customer-facing firewall guidance and add to Private Deployments onboarding doc (ETA 2025-11-20).
- Morgan: formalize runbook steps above and wire alert SRE-ctrlplane-conn-rate to include quick-links for tcpdump/pcap collection (ETA 2025-11-18).
- Infra team (assign): evaluate feasibility of optional pinned egress IP pools (COST-ANALYSIS-REQ, ETA 2026-01-15).

Notes to self / on-call tips (informal):
- When you see RST spikes, don’t assume TLS problem at first glance; confirm if RSTs coincide with NAT mapping changes.
- Keep the tcpdump window short (60–90s) and copy pcap to long-term storage immediately.
- For customer coordination, request their firewall change ticket id and look for any short windows where ephemeral ports were restricted.

Appendix — short sample debug session (commands run during incident):
- On control plane host: 
  - date; ss -s | head -n 10
  - sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 host 10.12.34.56 and port 443 -c 200 -w /tmp/10.12.34.56.443.pcap
  - sudo tcpdump -vvv -r /tmp/10.12.34.56.443.pcap | grep "RST" | wc -l
- From agent (customer): 
  - curl -v https://controlplane.redwood.local:443/health 2>&1 | tee /tmp/curl.out
  - sudo iptables -L -n -v | tee /tmp/iptables.out

Draft status: informal notes and working hypothesis. This should be converted into a formal postmortem and a short-runbook page in Confluence. Keep this doc as the single collection point for logs/pcaps before we redact customer-specific info for a public-facing postmortem.

End of draft.
